title: CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE. On the governance of God in general
latin: CAPUT VICESIMUM NONUM, De gubernatione DEI in genere. Creatione peracta Deus quievit, hoc est, novas rerum species condere haud perrexit, sed in conditis acquievit: sequitur gubernatio, quae est providentia Dei actualis, qua totum mundum conservat, regit, ordinat et singulas creaturas earumque actiones et passiones curat se decenter, illisque convenienter, ut nihil subsistats nec agat nec moveatur sine eo in hac rerum universitate, neque secus cadat quam ipsi visum, in bonum ipsarum creaturarum, praesertim piorum hominum, adque perfectionis divinae declarationem. Ordo enim postulat ut, postquam exsecuti sumus doctrinam de creatione tanquam regni Dei prima fundatione in tempore secundum aeternum ipsius consilium facta, quam sabbatum Dei excepit — Genesis 2:2; Exodus 20:11; Hebrews 4:4 — nunc accedamus ad gubernationem, ut liquet ex capitis 24 aphorismo 2, quae alias providentia actualis dici consuevit, et non significat aliquam Dei proprietatem, non qualitatem sive potentiam sive habitum, sed actum, qui non ad intra internus, sed ad extra et externus, circa obiectum aliud a Deo, idque non ut Deo ab aeterno in intellectione ipsius unitum, sed ut separatum et seorsim exsistens: actum, inquam, intellectus practici seu voluntatis intellectu utentis, non unico momento peractum, sed per momenta durationis continuum; quem intuitu potentem et continuum non male dixeris.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): whom by intuition you may not badly call powerful plus continuous — but through moments belonging toward duration continuous — not completed in a unique moment — an act namely belonging toward practical intellect or belonging toward will using intellect — but as separated plus existing apart — plus that not as united toward God from eternity in his intellection — around an object other from God — but toward outside plus external — which is not inward ad intra — but an act — nor habit nor power nor quality — nor does it signify some property belonging toward God — which otherwise has been accustomed to be called actual providence — as is clear from chapter 24 aphorism 2 — now let us approach toward governance — Genesis 2:2; Exodus 20:11; Hebrews 4:4 — which God's sabbath followed — made according toward his eternal counsel — as ye first foundation belonging toward God's kingdom in time — after we have executed ye doctrine concerning creation — for order demands. especially belonging toward pious humans, plus toward ye declaration belonging toward divine perfection — into ye good belonging toward ye creatures themselves — nor falls otherwise than seemed good toward him — so that nothing may subsist nor act nor be moved without him in this universe belonging toward things — conveniently toward them — by which he conserves, rules, orders ye whole world plus cares for singular creatures plus their actions plus passions decently — which is God's actual providence — governance follows — but he rested in things founded — he did not continue to found new species belonging toward things — Creation completed God rested, that is. CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE. On God's governance in general.
english: CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE. On the governance of God in general.

Creation finished, God rested — that is, He did not go on founding new species of things, but rested in what He had founded: there follows governance, which is God's actual providence, by which He conserves, rules, and orders the whole world and cares for each creature and its actions and passions, decently and as befits them, so that nothing in this universe of things subsists, acts, or is moved without Him, nor falls out otherwise than as seems good to Him, unto the good of the creatures themselves — especially of the godly — and unto the declaration of divine perfection.

For order requires that, after we have treated the doctrine of creation as the first foundation of God's kingdom in time according to His eternal counsel — which God's sabbath followed (Genesis 2:2; Exodus 20:11; Hebrews 4:4) — we now come to governance, as is clear from chapter 24, aphorism 2. Governance, otherwise commonly called actual providence, does not signify some property of God, nor a quality or power or habit, but an act — not inward and ad intra, but outward and external, about an object other than God, and that not as united to God from eternity in His intellection, but as separate and existing apart: an act, I say, of practical intellect or of will using the intellect, not finished in a single moment but continuous through the moments of duration; which, viewed as powerful and continuous, you may not badly so name.

title: Object of providence; necessary, contingent, rational, and irrational; God not author of sin
latin: Regit autem omnia universe — Nehemiah 9:6; Ephesians 4:6; Amos 3:6; Lamentations 3:37–38; Acts 17:25; Hebrews 1:3 — specialiter necessaria — Exodus 12:46; Job 19; Job 5:10; 37:5; 38:26–27; Psalm 104:13–14 — contingentia — Exodus 21:12–13; Job 1:21; Proverbs 16:1, 33; Matthew 10:29–30 — rationalia — Genesis 45:8; 50:20; Exodus 4:11; Job 12:6; 2 Samuel 16:10; Psalm 34:16, 21; Proverbs 21:1; Isaiah 10:5; Lamentations 3:37; Daniel 4:32; Acts 4:27–28 — expertia rationis — Job 37 toto; Psalm 104:9; Psalm 135:6–9 — ne secus cadat quicquam atque ipsi visum — 1 Samuel 2:25; Isaiah 8:10; Romans 8; 11:36; 1 Corinthians 9:9–10. Nec tamen ideo Deus ullius peccati auctor fiat — Genesis 18:25; Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 5:4–6; Jeremiah 19:5; Habakkuk 1:13; John 8:44; James 1:13, 17; 1 John 1:5. Regit interim etiam ea quibus per se casus inest — Exodus 21:13; Ecclesiastes 9:11; 1 Samuel 6:9. His et similibus testimoniis evincitur, obiectum providentiae non esse tantum caelestia et incorruptibilia, ut volebant illi — Job 22:12–14 — sed nullam rem sive superioris sive inferioris naturae excipiendam esse. Neque alienum est a Dei maiestate si etiam minutissima quaeque regat, cum omnium sit creator et dominus, neque sit humilis qui ad humilia respicit — Psalm 113:5–6 — et quanto maiore cura hominem prosequitur, tanto magis actiones eius subiiciuntur providentiae ipsius quam actiones rerum aliarum intellectu carentium — Psalm 33:14–15. Unde et corda, voluntates et actiones hominum in Dei manu, potestate ac dispositione, omnesque eventus et successus actionum nostrarum esse dicuntur — Proverbs 21:1; Genesis 45:8; Exodus 4:11; Isaiah 64:8; Philippians 2:13; Jeremiah 10:23; Proverbs 20:24. Neque enim in actionibus liberi arbitrii homo exemptus est ab ordine providentiae. Vide Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, Salvianum et alios.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): see Chrysostom, Theodoret, Salvian plus others — for neither in ye actions belonging toward free choice is humankind exempted from ye order belonging toward providence. Proverbs 21:1; Genesis 45:8; Exodus 4:11; Isaiah 64:8; Philippians 2:13; Jeremiah 10:23; Proverbs 20:24 — whence also hearts, wills plus humans' actions are said to be in God's hand, power plus disposition, plus all events plus successes belonging toward our actions. Psalm 33:14–15 — by so much more are his actions subjected toward his providence than ye actions belonging toward other things lacking intellect — plus by how much greater care he pursues humankind — Psalm 113:5–6 — nor is he humble who looks toward low things — since he is creator plus lord belonging toward all — nor is it alien from God's majesty if he also rules even ye least things. but no thing whether belonging toward superior or inferior nature is to be excepted — Job 22:12–14 — as those wished — ye object belonging toward providence is not only heavenly plus incorruptible things — by these plus similar testimonies it is proved. Exodus 21:13; Ecclesiastes 9:11; 1 Samuel 6:9 — meanwhile he also rules those things in which chance is present through itself. Genesis 18:25; Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 5:4–6; Jeremiah 19:5; Habakkuk 1:13; John 8:44; James 1:13, 17; 1 John 1:5 — nor nevertheless therefore does God become author belonging toward any sin. Especially necessary, contingent, rational, plus things lacking reason — he rules all things universally. CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE opening continued.
english: And He rules all things universally (Nehemiah 9:6; Ephesians 4:6; Amos 3:6; Lamentations 3:37–38; Acts 17:25; Hebrews 1:3) — specially the necessary (Exodus 12:46; Job 5:10; 37:5; 38:26–27; Psalm 104:13–14), the contingent (Exodus 21:12–13; Job 1:21; Proverbs 16:1, 33; Matthew 10:29–30), the rational (Genesis 45:8; 50:20; Exodus 4:11; 2 Samuel 16:10; Psalm 34:16, 21; Proverbs 21:1; Isaiah 10:5; Lamentations 3:37; Daniel 4:32; Acts 4:27–28), and things without reason (Job 37 throughout; Psalm 104:9; Psalm 135:6–9) — so that nothing falls out otherwise than as seems good to Him (1 Samuel 2:25; Isaiah 8:10; Romans 8; 11:36; 1 Corinthians 9:9–10).

Yet God does not thereby become the author of any sin (Genesis 18:25; Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 5:4–6; Jeremiah 19:5; Habakkuk 1:13; John 8:44; James 1:13, 17; 1 John 1:5). He also rules those things in which chance is present of itself (Exodus 21:13; Ecclesiastes 9:11; 1 Samuel 6:9). By these and like testimonies it is proved that the object of providence is not only heavenly and incorruptible things, as some wished (Job 22:12–14), but that no thing of higher or lower nature is to be excepted. Nor is it beneath God's majesty if He also rules the least things, since He is creator and Lord of all, and He is not made low who looks to low things (Psalm 113:5–6); and the greater care with which He pursues humankind, the more its actions are subject to His providence than the actions of things without intellect (Psalm 33:14–15). Whence hearts, wills, and human actions are said to be in God's hand, power, and disposition, and all the events and outcomes of our actions (Proverbs 21:1; Genesis 45:8; Exodus 4:11; Philippians 2:13; Jeremiah 10:23; Proverbs 20:24). For neither in the actions of free choice is humankind exempt from the order of providence. See Chrysostom, Theodoret, Salvian, and others.

title: II–VI: parts of governance; conservation immediate and mediate; notable observations
latin: II. Sunt autem in ea discernenda: 1. partes; 2. gradus; 3. magni in res creatas influxus. III. Primo, partes eius sunt conservatio et ordinatio. IV. CONSERVATIO est prima pars gubernationis, qua Deus res in mundo factas ut porro sint. Vide Psalmum 104 totum, quia qualis providentiae est speculum nitidissimum. Conservationi vero opponitur destructio, qua Deus substantiam aut accidens aliquod abolet. Conservatio est continuatio proprii esse formaliter. A quibus enim principiis emanat esse, ab eisdem continuari et servari oportet, non a contrariis, quia destruunt, non a diversis, quia nihil conferunt: sed simile simili servatur, praesertim potentiori, et quod est per participationem ens, ab eo quod per essentiam. Sicut enim ignis igni, frigus frigore per se, ens ente fovetur, maxime autem ab ente maximo, a quo habet ut sit. Idcirco scriptum est, ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia — id est, emanant, reguntur, servantur. Et Gregorius: Omnia, inquit, in nihilum redigerentur, nisi operatione divinae virtutis conservarentur. V. Est autem conservatio rerum immediata aut mediata, eaque directa aut indirecta. Nam Deus non solum per se res conservat, sed et per alias causas. VI. Sunt vero hic quaedam notabilia. 1. Deus conservat omnia principaliter; secundae autem causae secundario; eaeque priores Deoque viciniores sunt, magis conservant. 2. Quae a Deo solo fieri possunt per creationem neque aliter, ea non nisi a Deo possunt conservari. 3. Quoniam tanta est rerum multitudo diversissima, Deus necessitatem, fatum et harmoniam inseruit, quibus servarentur quanto tempore opus foret secunda entia, et ubi opus esset transmutarentur. 4. Distinxit Deus systemata plurima mutuo sese servantia moventiaque, ut rotae in horologio. 5. Res inferiores quandam habent sympathiam cum seminibus primis et superioribus.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): 5. Inferior things have a certain sympathy with first plus superior seeds. 4. God distinguished many systems mutually conserving plus moving one another, as wheels in a clock. 3. since so great is ye most diverse multitude belonging toward things, God inserted necessity, fate plus harmony. 2. Those which can be made by God alone through creation nor otherwise can be conserved only by God. 1. God conserves all things principally; second causes secondarily. VI. But here there are certain notables. For God not only conserves things through himself but also through other causes. V. But conservation belonging toward things is immediate or mediate, plus that direct or indirect. And Gregory: All things, he says, would be reduced into nothing unless they were conserved by ye operation belonging toward divine power. Romans 11:36 — therefore it is written, from him plus through him plus in him are all things. IV. CONSERVATION is ye first part belonging toward governance, by which God makes things in ye world so that they further are. III. First, its parts are conservation plus ordination. II. But in it there are to be discerned: 1. parts; 2. grades; 3. great influxes into created things.
english: II. In governance there are to be distinguished: (1) parts; (2) grades; (3) the great influxes into created things. III. First, its parts are conservation and ordination.

IV. CONSERVATION is the first part of governance, by which God makes things founded in the world so that they continue to be. See Psalm 104 throughout, a most clear mirror of such providence. Opposed to conservation is destruction, by which God abolishes some substance or accident. Conservation is the formal continuation of a thing's own being. For from the same principles from which being flows, it ought also to be continued and kept — not from contraries, which destroy, nor from diverse things, which contribute nothing: but like is kept by like, especially by the more powerful, and what is being by participation is kept by that which is being by essence. So fire is fostered by fire, cold by cold of itself, being by being — most of all by the greatest Being from whom it has that it is. Therefore it is written, from Him and through Him and in Him are all things (Romans 11:36) — that is, they emanate, are ruled, are kept. And Gregory: All things, he says, would be reduced to nothing unless conserved by the operation of divine power.

V. Conservation of things is immediate or mediate, and that direct or indirect. For God conserves things not only through Himself but also through other causes. VI. Here there are certain notables: (1) God conserves all things principally; second causes secondarily; and those nearer to God conserve more. (2) What can be made by God alone through creation, and not otherwise, can be conserved only by God. (3) Because the multitude of things is so great and diverse, God inserted necessity, fate, and harmony, by which second beings are kept as long as needed and transmuted when needed. (4) God distinguished many systems mutually keeping and moving one another, as wheels in a clock. (5) Inferior things have a certain sympathy with first and superior seeds.

title: VII–XVI: ordination — effectio, permissio, motio, cohibitio; ordinary and extraordinary; mediate and immediate
latin: VII. ORDINATIO est altera pars gubernationis, qua Deus omnia ad finem ultimum a se sapientissime praestitutum dirigit. VIII. Estque 1. effectio aut permissio; 2. motio aut cohibitio. IX. EFFECTIO divina est ordinatio, qua Deus omnis generis bona et mala poenae producit: eodemque sensu providentia efficiens dicitur. X. PERMISSIO divina est ordinatio, qua Deus sciens volens aliquid fieri sinit. Haec in primis spectat ad mala culpae, quae Deus ita permittit sive non impedit, ut ad finem optimum dirigat: ideoque et providentia permittens appellatur. XI. MOTIO divina est ordinatio, qua Deus omnes res ratione principii, medii et finis ita movet, ut motum vel efficiat et dirigat, vel tantum dirigat. XII. COHIBITIO divina est ordinatio, qua Deus actionem creaturae impedit. XIII. SECUNDO, quantum ad gradus et modos, gubernatio est 1. ordinaria vel extraordinaria, seu usitata aut inusitata. XIV. GUBERNATIO ORDINARIA est, qua Deus gubernat res eo ordine quem in prima creatione instituit. Hinc dicuntur res fieri secundum naturam, ex communi Dei beneplacito — Hosea 2:21–22; Acts 14:17; 17:25–28. XV. EXTRAORDINARIA est, qua Deus gubernat res aliter quam in prima creatione instituit. Hinc dicitur aliquid fieri supra aut praeter naturam, ex singulari dispensatione. Et hic excellit miraculum, quod est operatio Dei extraordinaria eaque evidens, totius naturae creatae vim excedens. XVI. Gubernatio est mediata aut immediata. Deus ea immediate gubernare dicitur quae regit non adhibitis mediis sive causis secundis; mediate, quae usurpato earum ministerio procurat. Concurrit tamen aliquando etiam circa idem opus aliqua immediata et mediata actio.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): yet sometimes also around ye same work some immediate plus mediate action concurs. mediately those which he procures by employing their ministry — God is said to govern immediately those which he rules without employing means or second causes. XVI. Governance is mediate or immediate. plus here miracle excels, which is God's extraordinary plus evident operation exceeding ye force belonging toward all created nature. XV. EXTRAORDINARY is that by which God governs things otherwise than he instituted in first creation. Hosea 2:21–22; Acts 14:17; 17:25–28 — XIV. ORDINARY GOVERNANCE is that by which God governs things in that order which he instituted in first creation. XIII. SECOND, as to grades plus modes, governance is 1. ordinary or extraordinary. XII. DIVINE RESTRAINT is ordination by which God impedes ye creature's action. XI. DIVINE MOTION. X. DIVINE PERMISSION. IX. DIVINE EFFECTING. VIII. And it is 1. effecting or permission; 2. motion or restraint. VII. ORDINATION is ye other part belonging toward governance.
english: VII. ORDINATION is the other part of governance, by which God directs all things to the last end most wisely appointed by Himself. VIII. And it is (1) effecting or permission; (2) motion or restraint.

IX. DIVINE EFFECTING is the ordination by which God produces goods of every kind and evils of punishment: in the same sense providence is called efficient. X. DIVINE PERMISSION is the ordination by which God, knowing and willing, lets something come to be. This looks chiefly to evils of fault, which God so permits or does not impede that He directs them to the best end: and therefore providence is also called permitting. XI. DIVINE MOTION is the ordination by which God so moves all things with respect to principle, means, and end that He either effects and directs the motion, or only directs it. XII. DIVINE RESTRAINT is the ordination by which God impedes a creature's action.

XIII. SECOND, as to grades and modes, governance is (1) ordinary or extraordinary, that is, customary or unusual. XIV. ORDINARY GOVERNANCE is that by which God governs things in the order He instituted in the first creation. Hence things are said to happen according to nature, from God's common good pleasure (Hosea 2:21–22; Acts 14:17; 17:25–28). XV. EXTRAORDINARY is that by which God governs things otherwise than He instituted in the first creation. Hence something is said to happen above or beside nature, from a singular dispensation. And here miracle excels: an extraordinary and evident operation of God exceeding the force of all created nature. XVI. Governance is mediate or immediate. God is said to govern immediately what He rules without second causes; mediately, what He procures by their ministry. Yet sometimes both an immediate and a mediate action concur about the same work.

title: XVII–XXI: general and special governance; merely corporeal creatures
latin: XVII. Tertio, est generalis aut specialis. XVIII. Gubernatio GENERALIS est, qua Deus gubernat res universas communiter. Dicitur etiam universalis, item communis providentia. Et haec non admittit magis et minus. XIX. Gubernatio SPECIALIS est, qua Deus gubernat res singulas naturis ipsarum convenienter. Haec etiam singularis providentia appellatur; et suos quosdam gradus habet. XX. Estque creaturarum mere corporearum, aut corporearum incorporearumque simul, aut incorporearum simpliciter, sive angelorum et hominum. XXI. Mere corporeas creaturas Deus minus quidem operose, sic tamen gubernat ut, quod illis datum, in eo ipsas aut conservet, aut sublimet, aut deprimat; altera iterum regit ita expertes, altera ut sentientes. Confer Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 104; 146:6–9; Psalm 147 totum; Isaiah 42:5; Acts 14:15–17; Job 36–41; Proverbs 6:6–8; Jeremiah 5:22; 8:7; Jonah 4:7; Matthew 5:45; 10:29.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Matthew 5:45; 10:29 — Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 104; 146:6–9; Psalm 147; Isaiah 42:5; Acts 14:15–17; Job 36–41; Proverbs 6:6–8; Jeremiah 5:22; 8:7; Jonah 4:7 — one again he rules as things without sense, another as sensing things — so nevertheless he governs that what was given toward them in that he either conserves or exalts or depresses them — XXI. Merely corporeal creatures God governs less laboriously indeed. XX. And it is belonging toward merely corporeal creatures, or corporeal plus incorporeal together, or incorporeal simply, whether belonging toward angels plus humans. XIX. SPECIAL governance is that by which God governs singular things conveniently toward their natures. XVIII. GENERAL governance is that by which God governs universal things commonly. XVII. Third, it is general or special.
english: XVII. Third, governance is general or special. XVIII. GENERAL governance is that by which God governs all things in common. It is also called universal, and likewise common providence; and this does not admit of more and less.

XIX. SPECIAL governance is that by which God governs singular things as befits their natures. This is also called singular providence, and it has certain grades of its own. XX. And it is of merely corporeal creatures, or of corporeal and incorporeal together, or of the incorporeal simply — that is, of angels and of humans.

XXI. Merely corporeal creatures God governs with less labor, yet so that what was given them He either conserves in them, or raises, or brings low; some again He rules as things without sense, others as things that sense. Compare Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 104; 146:6–9; Psalm 147 throughout; Isaiah 42:5; Acts 14:15–17; Job 36–41; Proverbs 6:6–8; Jeremiah 5:22; 8:7; Jonah 4:7; Matthew 5:45; 10:29.

title: XXII–XXXVII: governance of intelligent creatures by teaching — narration, law, promise, threat, covenant
latin: XXII. Intelligentium creaturarum gubernatio est, qua Deus eas regit partim docendo, partim agendo. Gubernat autem eas naturae suae convenienter — Genesis 28:15; Psalm 103:6–7, 11–12. XXIII. Docet autem Deus primo vel sine conditione, vel cum ea alias expressa alias tacita. XXIV. Deinde docet vel simpliciter extra rationem foederis, vel composite in foedere. XXV–XXVI. Simpliciter aliquid docet aut narrando aut circa creaturas aliquid definiendo. Narratio est qua Deus exponit tantum veritatem in rebus sciendis — doctrina simplex, prophetia, historia — cui respondere debet fides. XXVII. Narratio hic specialiter submonitio appellatur, quando Deus exponit veritatem in sciendis ad cautionem. XXVIII–XXXII. Porro circa intelligentes creaturas Deus aliquid definit dum iis quippiam lege designat — praecipiendo, interdicendo, vel concedendo — aut de iis aliquid pronunciat. Praeceptio docet sanctitatem in agendo; interdictio in re omittenda; concessio res medias pro libertate prudenter agendas omittendasque. XXXIII–XXXVI. Modus quo aliquid de creaturis pronunciat est vel promittendo vel comminando vel per indulgentiam. Promissio docet sententiam de benignitate; comminatio de severitate; indulgentia de nulla notabili benignitate neque severitate. XXXVII. Sequitur modus docendi composite, quo Deus cum creaturis intelligentibus foedus aliquod pangit, solemniter coniungens modos docendi et mutuam obligationem constituens.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): XXXVII. There follows ye composite mode belonging toward teaching by which God strikes some covenant with intelligent creatures. XXXIII–XXXVI. Promise teaches ye sentence concerning benignity; threat concerning severity; indulgence concerning no notable benignity nor severity. XXVIII–XXXII. Precept teaches holiness in doing; interdiction in a thing to be omitted; concession middle things for our liberty. XXV–XXVI. Simply he teaches either by narrating or by defining something around creatures — toward which faith ought to respond. XXIV. Then he teaches either simply outside ye reason belonging toward covenant, or compositely in covenant. XXIII. But God teaches first either without condition or with it. XXII. Governance belonging toward intelligent creatures is that by which God rules them partly by teaching, partly by doing.
english: XXII. The governance of intelligent creatures is that by which God rules them partly by teaching, partly by doing. And He governs them as befits their nature (Genesis 28:15; Psalm 103:6–7, 11–12).

XXIII. God teaches first either without condition, or with a condition sometimes expressed, sometimes tacit. XXIV. Then He teaches either simply, outside the reason of a covenant, or compositely, in a covenant. XXV–XXVI. Simply He teaches either by narrating or by defining something about creatures. Narration is that by which God only sets forth the truth in things to be known — simple doctrine, prophecy, history — to which faith ought to answer. XXVII. Narration is here specially called admonition when God sets forth truth in things to be known for caution.

XXVIII–XXXII. Further, about intelligent creatures God defines something when by law He designates something to them — by commanding, forbidding, or conceding — or pronounces something concerning them. Precept teaches holiness in doing; interdiction, holiness in omitting; concession, middle things to be done or omitted prudently for our liberty. XXXIII–XXXVI. The mode by which He pronounces something concerning creatures is by promising, by threatening, or by indulgence. Promise teaches His mind concerning kindness to be exercised; threat, concerning severity; indulgence, concerning neither notable kindness nor severity. XXXVII. There follows the composite mode of teaching, by which God strikes a covenant with intelligent creatures, solemnly joining modes of teaching and constituting mutual obligation.

title: XXXVIII–XLII: effecting, impeding, permitting, tolerating; Cap. 29 close
latin: XXXVIII. Atque hactenus vidimus quomodo Deus creaturas intelligentes docere soleat etiam composite: nunc sequitur quomodo aliquid circa easdem impleat, et quidem vel efficiendo vel impediendo vel permittendo vel tolerando. Cum Deus creaturas intelligentes docuit, si agant aut omittant tunc quod debent aut quomodo debent, earum obsequia a Deo approbantur ut bona aut licita; sin, improbantur ut illicita. XXXIX. EFFECTIO est qua Deus ea efficit quorum vera causa est, sive benefaciendo sive affligendo — Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 18:27; 57:3–4; 116:7; Exodus 23:22; Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Haggai 1:6; Psalm 80; 90. XL. IMPEDITIO est qua Deus ea quae vult subtrahit creaturae in conservatione aut concursu, fortioremque vim aliquando infirmiori opponit, aut infirmiorem praeter ordinem roborat, ut valentiorem sistere aut propulsare possit — Genesis 26:6; Isaiah 37:29; Acts 16:6–7. XLI. PERMISSIO est qua Deus quasdam creaturas arbitrio relinquit. Non impedit enim aliquando creaturas quo minus agant ex sese, sibi aliquantulum relictae — Job 1:12; 1 Kings 22:21–22; Acts 14:16. Cum autem Deus eas permittit arbitrio ipsarum, fit ut, si non considerate satis sua sapientia et prudentia utantur, sua culpa in peccatum incidant. XLII. TOLERATIO est qua Deus creaturam suam neque poena afficit neque etiam notabili beneficio. Vide Methodum Matthiae Martinii Herbornae editam et epitomen theologiae methodicae libro 3 capite 2–3 hic impressam.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): see Matthias Martini's Method published at Herborn plus ye epitome belonging toward methodical theology book 3 chapter 2–3 here printed. XLII. TOLERATION is that by which God neither afflicts his creature with punishment nor even with notable benefit. XLI. PERMISSION is that by which God leaves certain creatures toward their choice — Job 1:12; 1 Kings 22:21–22; Acts 14:16. XL. IMPEDING — Genesis 26:6; Isaiah 37:29; Acts 16:6–7. XXXIX. EFFECTING — Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28. XXXVIII. Thus far we have seen how God is accustomed to teach intelligent creatures even compositely: now there follows how he fulfills something around ye same, either by effecting or impeding or permitting or tolerating.  for when God has taught intelligent creatures if they act or omit as they ought their obediences are approved as good or lawful else disapproved as unlawful. Effecting brings about those things of which God is true cause whether by benefiting or by afflicting as Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 and many Psalms show. Impeding withdraws in conservation or concurrence what God wills and sometimes sets a stronger force against a weaker or beyond order strengthens the weaker so it can stop or drive back the stronger as Genesis 26 Isaiah 37 and Acts 16 show. Permission leaves certain creatures toward their own choice so that if they do not use wisdom and prudence considerately enough they fall into sin by their own fault as Job 1 First Kings 22 and Acts 14 show. Toleration neither afflicts with punishment nor even with notable benefit and Matthias Martini Method plus epitome book three chapters two and three are cited for fuller method.
english: XXXVIII. Thus far we have seen how God is accustomed to teach intelligent creatures even compositely: now there follows how He fulfills something concerning the same — namely by effecting, or impeding, or permitting, or tolerating. When God has taught intelligent creatures, if they then do or omit what they ought and as they ought, their obedience is approved by God as good or lawful; if not, it is disapproved as unlawful.

XXXIX. EFFECTING is that by which God brings about those things of which He is the true cause, whether by doing good or by afflicting (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 18:27; 57:3–4; 116:7; Exodus 23:22; Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Haggai 1:6; Psalm 80; 90). XL. IMPEDING is that by which God withdraws from the creature in conservation or concurrence what He wills, and sometimes opposes a stronger force to a weaker, or beyond order strengthens the weaker so that it can stop or drive back the stronger (Genesis 26:6; Isaiah 37:29; Acts 16:6–7).

XLI. PERMISSION is that by which God leaves certain creatures to their own choice. For sometimes He does not impede creatures from acting of themselves, left a little to themselves (Job 1:12; 1 Kings 22:21–22; Acts 14:16). And when God permits them to their own choice, it comes about that if they do not use their wisdom and prudence considerately enough, they fall into sin by their own fault. XLII. TOLERATION is that by which God neither afflicts His creature with punishment nor even with notable benefit. See Matthias Martini's Method published at Herborn and the epitome of methodical theology, book 3, chapters 2–3, printed here.
